explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. “Follow Me,” He tells Levi, the man sitting at the tax booth. Two words, no speech, no sales pitch. I've watched bakers take longer picking a cookie shape. And Levi got up and followed Him.

Jesus doesn't say anything about the booth. What He tells Levi is “Follow Me.” Levi was sitting at the tax booth when Jesus saw him, and the text says he got up and followed Him. It keeps the invitation short and simple.

Good guess, because Jesus taught the people beside the sea earlier in this passage. But to Levi, the man at the tax booth, He says something different: “Follow Me.” It's a call to come along with Him, not just to listen. The text says Levi got up and followed Him.

The text never shows Levi asking for any time. Jesus tells him, “Follow Me,” and Levi got up and followed Him. No request for time is mentioned anywhere. I'd probably have asked for a minute to check my oven timer.
Right, the text shows no request at all. Jesus says “Follow Me,” and Levi got up and followed Him. There's no gap in the story for thinking it over. It goes straight from the call to the following.

That's the guest list, friend. Many tax collectors and sinners were eating with Jesus and His disciples at Levi's house. The text adds that there were many who followed Him. Levi doesn't host a small dinner, he hosts a FULL one.

The text doesn't name shepherds or farmers at this dinner. It says many tax collectors and sinners were eating with Jesus and His disciples. It also says there were many who followed Him. So the people at Levi's table are the ones the text names.

Nice crafty crowd, but potters and weavers aren't in this passage. The text says many tax collectors and sinners were eating with Jesus and His disciples at Levi's house. It also says there were many who followed Him.
Yes, the scribes who were Pharisees. They see Jesus eating with tax collectors and sinners, and they have a question about it. Notice what the text says about who they ask.
Priests aren't named here. The text says it's the scribes who were Pharisees who see Jesus eating with tax collectors and sinners. They're the ones with the question about this dinner.
Elders aren't mentioned in this scene. The text says the scribes who were Pharisees saw Jesus eating with these people. They're the ones who ask the question about the meal.

Look again at who gets asked. The scribes who were Pharisees ask His disciples, “Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?” They don't ask Jesus to His face. But the next verse says that on hearing this, Jesus answers them.

Right, they don't ask Jesus Himself. The scribes who were Pharisees ask His disciples, “Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?” It's a question about Him, asked of the others. Then, on hearing this, Jesus tells them His answer.

Yes, the sick. Jesus says, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.” He uses a picture everybody gets, because everybody knows why people go see a doctor. Then He says, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”
It's actually the other way around. Jesus says, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.” Healthy people can skip the waiting room. The sick are the ones who need the doctor.

Money doesn't come into it. Jesus says, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.” So the picture is about sickness and health, not who has what in the bank. He then says, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

That's it, friend. Jesus says, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” He says it right after, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.” And it's His answer to the scribes who were Pharisees, who had asked His disciples why He eats with tax collectors and sinners.

“Wise” sounds like a good word to put there, but it's not what Jesus says. His words are, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” He had just said it's the sick who need a doctor. This is who He came to call.

It's a big-sounding word, but Jesus doesn't use it here. He says, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” That line comes right after His picture of the doctor and the sick. He came to call sinners.

Yes. John's disciples and the Pharisees were often fasting, so people came to Jesus and asked, “Why don’t Your disciples fast like John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees?” They bring the question straight to Him. And He answers with a wedding.

It's true, actually. The text says people came to Jesus and asked, “Why don’t Your disciples fast like John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees?” John's disciples and the Pharisees were often fasting. So the question is about His disciples not fasting like those two groups.

Yes, friend. Jesus says, “How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them? As long as He is with them, they cannot fast.” The bridegroom is right there with them. So it's no time for fasting.
Jesus doesn't mention before the wedding. He says the guests cannot fast “As long as He is with them…” It's about whether the bridegroom is with them. That's the timing He gives.

Jesus doesn't say anything about guests going home. He says they cannot fast “As long as He is with them…” The fasting He talks about comes when the bridegroom is taken from them. That's a different moment.

explanations.answer: He will be taken from them
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says. “But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them…” The picture changes here. First He says, “As long as He is with them, they cannot fast.” and then He looks ahead to a time still coming.

Jesus doesn't say anything about more guests. What He says is, “…the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them…” The change is about the bridegroom being taken from the guests. And that's the moment He says they will fast.

explanations.answer: He will start a new feast
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't mention a new feast here. He says, “…the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them…” That's the change for the guests. After that, He says, they will fast.

Yes. Jesus says, “…the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.” First He says they cannot fast while the bridegroom is with them. Then He gives the time when they will.

It's true, friend. Jesus says, “…the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.” Before that, He says, they cannot fast while He is with them. So the fasting comes after the bridegroom is taken.

explanations.answer: The new piece pulls away and the tear gets worse
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says. If someone sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, “…the new piece will pull away from the old, and a worse tear will result.” So the fix makes things worse. I tie my apron with my mustache, but even I can follow that.

explanations.answer: The patch shrinks down to a perfect fit
explanations.explanation: It sounds like a happy ending, but Jesus says something else. The new piece “…will pull away from the old, and a worse tear will result.” The patch is unshrunk cloth, and it's the new piece that pulls away.

explanations.answer: The old cloth turns as strong as new
explanations.explanation: I wish that worked on my edges! But Jesus doesn't say that. He says the new piece “…will pull away from the old, and a worse tear will result.” The old garment ends up with a bigger tear.

Jesus says the opposite. He says, “No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment.” He's describing something people don't do. Then He says what would happen if someone did: the new piece would pull away and a worse tear would result.

Right, friend. Jesus says, “No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment.” It's something people don't do. And He adds that if someone did, the new piece would pull away from the old, and a worse tear would result.
Yes. Jesus says, “…no one pours new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins…” Old wineskins and new wine don't go together. Then He tells what to do instead.

explanations.answer: The skins make the wine better

Yes, ruined. Jesus says the wine will burst the skins, “…and both the wine and the wineskins will be ruined.” Nobody comes out ahead. Both are lost.
I'd love a happy ending like that, friend, but Jesus says something else. He says, “…both the wine and the wineskins will be ruined.” The skins burst. And the wine is lost with them.

Nobody gets a second pour here. Jesus says the wine will burst the skins, “…and both the wine and the wineskins will be ruined.” Both are lost. Then He says what to do instead: new wine is poured into new wineskins.
